text: Iraq is working with the UAE's ADNOC Group and other international traders to keep crude exports moving through the Strait of Hormuz as Baghdad looks to protect key oil revenue amid ongoing Gulf shipping disruptions.  Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organization (SOMO) stated that ADNOC is among the firms buying Iraqi oil and successfully moving shipments through the strait, with its trading arm supplying Iraqi crude to Asian refiners via a shuttle system that reduces the risk of sending larger tankers into the Gulf.  ➡️ Under the arrangement, smaller vessels carry Iraqi Basrah oil through Hormuz before transferring cargo to larger tankers bound for Asia, with tracking devices sometimes switched off along parts of the route given the tense maritime environment.  ➡️ The deal offers Iraq a critical lifeline while standard tanker operations remain constrained, as Baghdad also pursues longer-term export routes through Turkey and the Mediterranean to reduce its dependence on Hormuz.  🔗 https://www.iraqinews.com/iraq/uaes-adnoc-helps-keep-iraqi-oil-flowing-through-strait-of-hormuz/

text: CBC News Network, Aug 11 2026: “A crucial trade meeting is underway this hour in Washington… It’s the third round of trade negotiations in as many weeks… with just 8 days to go until President Donald Trump’s new tariff deadline… This is a PIVOTAL time… really crunch time… sources have told us that this period constitutes a bit of a cliff for Canada”  Reality check: Canada remains well behind Mexico. The US and Mexico already finished three formal multi-day bilateral rounds on the USMCA review (May, June, and July 2026) and have a fourth set for September. Those talks were described as months more advanced, with systematic progress on rules of origin, steel, aluminum, autos, and economic security  Meanwhile, Canada’s process stayed deliberately and largely informal until the recent tariff-driven scramble of high-level meetings. CBC’s breathless framing of today’s session as make-or-break “crunch time” highlights the late urgency while downplaying how much further along the Mexico track has been  And at this “crucial” moment—with an August 19 tariff deadline looming—Prime Minister Mark Carney is on personal vacation in Italy. His team is handling the talks; he says he’s staying in contact. Optics aside, the contrast with the intensity CBC is pushing is hard to miss  “Buy Canadian / Travel Canadian” messaging is strong for the public. Carney travel schedule and destination tells its own story  @brodiefenlon @MarkJCarney

text: $VLO $MPC $PSX $DINO Hydrocarbon Infrastructure at War: Refinery Outages, Storage Damage and Read-Throughs. New: 8/10/26.  The global refining system is operating under a stress profile that the physical damage statistics alone significantly understate. Effective unavailable capacity — accounting for precautionary shutdowns, utility failures, and logistical disruption alongside direct hardware damage — is materially higher than the percentage of physically impaired assets would suggest. That distinction is critical for understanding why refined product markets are tighter than a facilities-damage assessment implies.  Russia's refining deficit is the most structurally persistent supply disruption in the current environment. Repeated strikes on secondary conversion units — the catalytic crackers and hydrotreaters that upgrade atmospheric distillate into higher-value products — have created a production gap that simple crude throughput restoration cannot address. Secondary unit repair timelines are measured in months to years, not weeks, and the combination of sanctions-constrained equipment sourcing and ongoing strike risk makes restoration timelines genuinely uncertain rather than merely delayed. The practical effect is a persistent Russian middle distillate shortfall that cannot be quickly reversed regardless of how the broader conflict trajectory evolves.  The Gulf region disruption is structurally different — a multifaceted shock affecting crude production, export terminal operations, and shipping route availability simultaneously. Each layer compounds the others: reduced crude availability limits refinery throughput globally, export terminal disruption concentrates the supply shock geographically, and shipping route displacement increases voyage costs and transit times in ways that create effective supply tightness beyond the production volume impact alone.  Middle distillate crack spreads at record levels are the price signal reflecting the specific product mix consequence of these disruptions. Diesel and jet fuel are disproportionately affected because secondary conversion capacity — exactly what has been most damaged in Russia — is what converts atmospheric crude fractions into middle distillates at scale. The global refining system cannot easily substitute for that lost conversion capacity in the near term regardless of crude availability.  Inventory drawdowns are the cumulative financial expression of the supply-demand imbalance, and declining inventory levels reduce the buffer that typically moderates price volatility during supply disruptions. A structurally tight market with low inventories and constrained restoration timelines is the condition that sustains elevated crack spreads rather than normalizing them — and the repair complexity, sanctions constraints, and ongoing conflict dynamics suggest that restoration will be slower and less complete than historical disruption recovery patterns would predict.

text: "All recent Yanbu crude loadings conducted without AIS signals Dark voyages create wide discrepancies in Saudi export estimates Saudi crude loadings from Egypt's Sidi Kerir hit record: Vortexa.   Saudi crude ​exports from the Red Sea are increasingly vanishing from view as tankers switch off tracking signals to avoid attacks ‌by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis, with analysts saying all recent Yanbu loadings have been conducted "dark". The Houthis declared a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia on July 20, opening a new front against the United States and its allies in the Iran war.  Since then, they have claimed attacks on Saudi-linked tankers, Yanbu oil facilities and, ​most recently, the Jazan refinery on the Red Sea coast, prompting more vessels to operate without publicly visible tracking data.  The growing use ​of so-called dark voyages is clouding visibility into Saudi oil exports, making it harder to assess the ⁠degree to which the Houthi threats may be disrupting crude flows. Ship-tracking firms have produced widely differing export estimates - data which is used ​by the International Energy Agency, OPEC and traders to assess global oil supply and forecast market trends. In the week beginning August 3, data ​analytics firm Vortexa estimated Yanbu loadings fell to 2.38 million barrels per day from 2.71 million the previous week, while Kpler estimated a sharper drop to 1.78 million bpd from 4.04 million, and AXSMarine calculated a rise to 850,000 bpd from about 420,000 bpd.  CONDUCTED ​DARK Those trying to monitor shipments rely on a vessel re-appearing on tracking systems once it has left the high-risk area, using satellite ​data to cross-check movements and try to fill in the gaps.  Kpler analyst Nhway Khin Soe said about 70% of Saudi west coast loadings over the past few weeks were dark. Shipping traffic through the Bab al-Mandeb Strait at the southern tip of the Red Sea had already been affected by two years of sporadic Houthi attacks ​on commercial shipping. An average ​of 32 vessels a day ⁠transited the waterway last week, according to Kpler data, down from about 50 a day before the group announced its latest blockade.  Ship-tracking data shows that Saudi Arabia has been sending more oil north through ​the Red Sea, either via the Suez Canal or Egypt's SUMED pipeline, which links Ain Sokhna ​on the Red ⁠Sea to Sidi Kerir on the Mediterranean coast. Crude and condensate loadings at Sidi Kerir averaged a record 2.17 million bpd last week, around 50% higher than the previous week, with about 90% of the total volumes Saudi crude, Vortexa's Morris said.  The cost of war risk insurance has jumped in ⁠recent days ​and tanker companies are also shifting their sailing strategies. Major tanker operator DHT previously ​exited the Red Sea via Bab al-Mandeb when lifting oil." https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/saudi-red-sea-oil-exports-go-dark-houthi-attack-threat-grows-2026-08-12/
